question: In GREML, what does the genetic relationship matrix (GRM) measure for each pair of people?

answers.answer: How similar their genotypes are across all genotyped SNPs
answers.feedback: Right. Each entry is a genome-wide correlation between two people's standardized genotypes; for unrelated people it is close to 0.

answers.answer: How similar their trait values are
answers.feedback: Trait similarity is what GREML relates to the GRM; the GRM itself is computed from genotypes only.

answers.answer: Whether they are related according to a family pedigree
answers.feedback: GREML measures relatedness from SNP data, and close relatives are usually removed from the analysis.

answers.answer: The P-value of each SNP
answers.feedback: GREML does not test SNPs one at a time; it uses all SNPs together to measure genetic similarity.

question: An LD score regression gives an intercept of 1.20 and a clearly positive slope. What does the intercept suggest?

answers.answer: Some inflation of the test statistics from confounding, such as population stratification
answers.feedback: Right. Confounding raises χ² equally at every LD score, which lifts the intercept above 1. The slope reflects true polygenic signal.

answers.answer: The SNP-heritability is 1.20
answers.feedback: SNP-heritability comes from the slope (scaled by M/N), not the intercept, and cannot exceed 1.

answers.answer: The study has no true associations
answers.feedback: A clearly positive slope indicates real polygenic signal tagged in proportion to LD.

answers.answer: Nothing: the intercept is always above 1
answers.feedback: Without confounding the expected intercept is 1. Values well above 1 point to confounding (or cryptic relatedness).

question: Why are close relatives removed before running GREML?

answers.answer: Relatives share family environment, which could be mistaken for genetic similarity
answers.feedback: Right. Using only unrelated people means trait similarity can be attributed to genetic similarity measured from SNPs, not to a shared upbringing.

answers.answer: Relatives cannot be genotyped on the same array
answers.feedback: Relatives can be genotyped like anyone else; the concern is shared environment.

answers.answer: GREML only works with exactly zero genetic similarity
answers.feedback: GREML relies on the small, non-zero genetic similarities between unrelated people.

answers.answer: Relatives always have the same phenotype
answers.feedback: Relatives differ in their phenotypes; the problem is that their similarity partly reflects shared environment.

question: In LD score regression, why does a SNP with a high LD score tend to have a larger χ² statistic when a trait is polygenic?

answers.answer: It is correlated with many other variants, so it is more likely to tag causal variants
answers.feedback: Right. With causal variants scattered across the genome, SNPs that tag more variation pick up more of the signal.

answers.answer: High-LD SNPs are always causal
answers.feedback: LD score measures how much variation a SNP tags, not whether it is causal.

answers.answer: High-LD SNPs are genotyped more accurately
answers.feedback: The relationship comes from tagging causal variation, not from genotyping accuracy.

answers.answer: Population stratification affects only high-LD SNPs
answers.feedback: Stratification inflates SNPs roughly equally regardless of LD, which is why it shows up in the intercept, not the slope.

question: An LD score regression of a GWAS of 50,000 people at 1,000,000 SNPs gives a slope of 0.015. What is the SNP-heritability? (Give two decimal places and press Enter.)

answers.feedback: Right. The slope is N·h²_SNP / M, so h²_SNP = slope × M / N = 0.015 × 1,000,000 / 50,000 = 0.30.
That is the slope itself. Multiply by M / N to convert it to h²_SNP.
You multiplied by N / M. The slope equals N·h²/M, so h² = slope × M / N.
Slope = N·h²_SNP / M, so h²_SNP = slope × M / N.

question: Which situation favours LD score regression over GREML?

answers.answer: Only summary statistics from a large meta-analysis are available
answers.feedback: Right. LD score regression needs only summary statistics and a reference LD panel; GREML needs individual-level genotypes.

answers.answer: Individual genotypes are available for 5,000 people
answers.feedback: With individual-level data, GREML is usually more precise for the same sample size.

answers.answer: The GWAS is of an admixed population with no matching LD reference panel
answers.feedback: That is a weakness of LD score regression, which needs LD scores that match the GWAS ancestry.

answers.answer: You want the most precise estimate from a small sample
answers.feedback: LD score regression is less precise than GREML and works best with very large GWAS.

question: Which is NOT a likely reason that SNP-heritability is lower than twin heritability?

answers.answer: GWAS participants have no genetic variation
answers.feedback: Right, this is not a reason (and it is false). Real reasons include untagged rare variants and possible overestimation of twin heritability.

answers.answer: Rare variants are not well tagged by genotyping arrays
answers.feedback: This is a real reason: h²_SNP only captures variation tagged by the SNPs used.

answers.answer: Twin studies may overestimate heritability, for example if MZ twins share more environment than DZ twins
answers.feedback: This is a real possibility: violations of the equal environments assumption can inflate twin estimates.

answers.answer: Twin heritability can include non-additive genetic effects
answers.feedback: This is a real reason: SNP-based methods capture additive effects of common variants.
